title: Which data collection method?
intro: The right method depends on whether you need numbers or reasons, and whether the data already exists somewhere.

q1.text: Does the data you need already exist somewhere?

options.label: Yes, published by an organization that offers programmatic access
Yes, but only as web pages with no API
Yes, as an existing dataset (a repository, internal records, a census)
No, I have to collect it from people or events

q2.text: What kind of answer do you need?

options.label: Numbers from many people: how many, how much, how satisfied
Reasons and experiences from a few people: why and how
Whether a change causes a difference in behaviour

l_api.title: Use the API
l_api.detail: An API returns structured data (usually JSON) under documented terms and rate limits. It is more stable and more clearly permitted than scraping.

l_scrape.title: Web scraping, done ethically
l_scrape.detail: Check the terms of service and robots.txt, rate-limit requests, identify your scraper, and avoid personal data without a lawful basis. Expect pages to change and break your parser.

l_secondary.title: Secondary data
l_secondary.detail: Fast and cheap, but collected for someone else's purpose: check its documentation, licence, coverage and quality before relying on it.

l_survey.title: Survey
l_survey.detail: Closed questions and rating scales give quantitative data that scales cheaply. Use neutral, single-topic questions, pilot the survey, and sample so respondents represent the population (for example stratified random sampling).

l_interview.title: Interviews
l_interview.detail: Qualitative depth from a small group. Structured interviews (same questions, same order) keep answers comparable; semi-structured ones allow follow-ups.

l_experiment.title: Experiment (A/B test)
l_experiment.detail: Randomly assign people to versions and compare outcomes. Random assignment is what lets you claim causation.

title: Where should this data live?
intro: Storage choices follow from how structured the data is, how big it gets, and who uses it for what.

q1.text: What is the data used for?

options.label: Running the business day to day: orders, payments, account updates
Analysis and reporting across the business
A one-off analysis or a small table shared with a few people

q2.text: What does the data look like when it arrives?

options.label: Cleaned, structured tables feeding dashboards and SQL reports
Raw data of many kinds (logs, JSON, images, audio) kept for future use and ML

q3.text: Does it need formulas, several sheets or formatting for people to read?

options.label: Yes
No, just a portable table for code and other tools

l_oltp.title: Relational (OLTP) database
l_oltp.detail: Built for many small, concurrent reads and writes with constraints that protect integrity. Don't run heavy analytical queries against it.

l_warehouse.title: Data warehouse
l_warehouse.detail: Cleaned, integrated, structured data with the schema defined before loading (schema-on-write), optimized for SQL analytics and BI.

l_lake.title: Data lake
l_lake.detail: Raw data in native formats with schema-on-read, on cheap cloud object storage. Needs governance and metadata or it becomes a data swamp.

l_excel.title: Excel workbook
l_excel.detail: Sheets, formulas and formatting for human readers; limited to 1,048,576 rows per sheet and awkward for concurrent editing.

l_csv.title: CSV file
l_csv.detail: Plain text that every tool reads. No types, no formulas, one table per file; state the delimiter and encoding.

title: How should I handle these missing values?
intro: Start with why values are missing, then with what kind of column it is.

q1.text: Is the missing value the target you are trying to predict?

options.label: Yes
No, it's a feature or a descriptive column
Pure chance: a glitch unrelated to anything (MCAR)
It depends on other recorded columns, e.g. younger people skip it (MAR)
It depends on the value itself, e.g. high earners hide income (MNAR)

q3.text: How much is missing, and what kind of column is it?

options.label: A few rows in a large dataset
A numeric column with outliers or skew
A roughly symmetric numeric column
A categorical column
An ordered time series

l_drop_target.title: Exclude those rows from training
l_drop_target.detail: A model can't learn from rows without a label, and imputing the target invents answers.

l_mar.title: Impute using the related columns
l_mar.detail: Group-wise statistics, regression or multiple imputation use the observed variables that drive the missingness.

l_mnar.title: Model it, flag it, or collect more
l_mnar.detail: Deletion and simple imputation are both biased. Add a missing-indicator column, use domain knowledge or a model of the missingness, and state the limitation.

l_drop.title: Drop the rows
l_drop.detail: With MCAR data and few missing rows, deletion is unbiased and simple; it only costs a little statistical power.

l_median.title: Impute with the median
l_median.detail: The median is robust to outliers and skew; the mean would be pulled toward the extremes.

l_mean.title: Impute with the mean
l_mean.detail: Fine for symmetric data, but it shrinks the variance; add a flag column if that matters.

l_mode.title: Impute with the mode, or an "Unknown" category
l_mode.detail: The most frequent category keeps the column valid; "Unknown" keeps the fact that it was missing.

l_ffill.title: Forward-fill or interpolate
l_ffill.detail: In ordered data the previous value (or a line between neighbours) is the best estimate.

title: Scale, encode or bin this column?
intro: Numeric columns get scaled or binned; categorical columns get encoded. The details depend on order and outliers.

q1.text: What kind of column is it?

options.label: Numeric
Categorical
Values on a fixed 0-to-1 range, no big outliers
Centred values for a model; outliers present or range unbounded
Groups such as age bands instead of exact numbers

q3.text: Do the categories have a natural order?

options.label: No (colour, city, product type)
Yes (low < medium < high)
It's the target label of a classifier

q4.text: How should the bins be defined?

options.label: By meaningful edges I choose (0–18, 19–64, 65+)
So each bin holds about the same number of rows (quartiles)

l_minmax.title: Min-max scaling
l_minmax.detail: (x − min) / (max − min) maps values to [0, 1]. Fit on training data only.

l_zscore.title: Z-score standardization
l_zscore.detail: (x − mean) / std gives mean 0 and std 1. Less squashed by outliers than min-max; robust scaling (median and IQR) resists them further.
l_zscore.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)
X_test_s = scaler.transform(X_test)

l_onehot.title: One-hot encoding
l_onehot.detail: One indicator column per category, so no false order is implied. Watch out for high-cardinality columns.

l_ordinal.title: Ordinal mapping
l_ordinal.detail: Map categories to integers that follow the real order, so models can use it.

l_label.title: Label encoding
l_label.detail: Integer codes are fine for a target label; the classifier treats them as classes, not quantities.

l_cut.title: pd.cut
l_cut.detail: Bins by the edges you give; intervals are right-closed by default and values outside the edges become NaN.

l_qcut.title: pd.qcut
l_qcut.detail: Bins by quantiles, so each bin has about the same count.

title: Which validation check catches this?
intro: Name the check by what the rule compares a value against.

q1.text: What does the rule compare the value against?

options.label: Its expected kind of value (integer, date, text)
Allowed limits (0 to 120) or a fixed list of values
A pattern (email, postcode, ISO date)
Another field in the same record
Values in another table or reference list
Other rows of the same column (no repeats)

l_type.title: Type check
l_type.detail: Confirms the data type; put it early in ingestion so bad files fail fast.
l_type.code:
if not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df["qty"]):
    raise TypeError("qty must be numeric")

l_range.title: Range / allowed-values check
l_range.detail: Confirms a value lies within limits or belongs to a set.

l_format.title: Format check
l_format.detail: Confirms the value matches a pattern, usually with a regular expression.

l_crossfield.title: Cross-field check
l_crossfield.detail: Compares fields within one record, such as dates in order or a total matching its parts.

l_crossref.title: Cross-reference (referential) check
l_crossref.detail: Confirms the value exists elsewhere, the job a foreign key does inside a database.

l_unique.title: Uniqueness check
l_unique.detail: Confirms keys are not repeated; the job a primary key does inside a database.

title: Which file format and reader?
intro: Choose by the shape of the data, then use the matching reader.

options.label: Flat rows and columns
Nested objects and lists, as an API returns
A tree of tagged elements with attributes
Free text with no structure

q2.text: Is it a plain table or a workbook with several sheets?

options.label: A plain table
A workbook

l_csv.title: CSV
l_csv.detail: `pd.read_csv(path, sep=",", encoding="utf-8")`; write with `df.to_csv(path, index=False)`. Everything is text until parsed.

l_json.title: JSON
l_json.detail: `json.load(f)` for a file, `json.loads(s)` for a string; `pd.json_normalize` flattens nested records into columns.
l_json.code:
import json
with open("orders.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
df = pd.json_normalize(data["orders"])

l_xml.title: XML
l_xml.detail: `xml.etree.ElementTree`: `findall` for elements, `.text` for content, `.get()` for attributes; or `pd.read_xml` for simple row-like XML.
l_xml.code:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
root = ET.parse("books.xml").getroot()
titles = [b.find("title").text for b in root.findall("book")]

l_txt.title: TXT
l_txt.detail: `open(path, encoding="utf-8")` and iterate line by line; extract structure with string methods or regular expressions.
l_txt.code:
with open("log.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    errors = [line for line in f if "ERROR" in line]

title: Which Python data structure?
intro: Pick the structure by how you will look things up and whether the data changes.

q1.text: How will you mostly access the data?

options.label: By a key, such as a customer ID
By asking "is this item in the collection?", or removing duplicates
In order, by position

q2.text: Will the collection change after it is created?

options.label: Yes: items are added, removed or sorted
No: it's a fixed record, or it must be usable as a dict key

l_dict.title: dict
l_dict.detail: Maps unique, hashable keys to values with fast lookup; insertion-ordered. Use `.get()` to avoid KeyError.

l_set.title: set
l_set.detail: Unordered unique items with fast membership tests and set algebra (`|`, `&`, `-`). An empty set is `set()`.

l_tuple.title: tuple
l_tuple.detail: Ordered and immutable; hashable when its items are, so it can be a dict key. One item needs a comma: `(5,)`.

title: Which exception will this raise?
intro: Most exam error questions come down to one of these.

options.label: An operation got a value of the wrong type, e.g. "3" + 4
The type is right but the value is bad, e.g. int("12a")
Something being looked up doesn't exist
Division by zero
Importing a package that isn't installed
A dict key or a DataFrame column
A list or tuple position
An attribute or method, e.g. None.split()
A variable name that was never defined
A file path

l_type.title: TypeError
l_type.detail: Wrong type for the operation, or a function called with the wrong arguments.

l_value.title: ValueError
l_value.detail: Right type, inappropriate value. `pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce")` avoids it by producing NaN.

l_zero.title: ZeroDivisionError
l_zero.detail: Division or modulo by zero with Python numbers. (NumPy and pandas don't raise: they return inf or NaN, and NumPy also prints a RuntimeWarning.)

l_module.title: ModuleNotFoundError
l_module.detail: A subclass of ImportError; fix with `pip install` in the right environment.

l_key.title: KeyError
l_key.detail: Missing dict key or DataFrame column; `dict.get()` or checking `in` avoids it.

l_index.title: IndexError
l_index.detail: Position out of range; valid indexes run from 0 to len − 1 (or −len to −1).

l_attr.title: AttributeError
l_attr.detail: The object has no such attribute; often a variable is unexpectedly None (for example after an `inplace=True` call).

l_name.title: NameError
l_name.detail: The name isn't defined in any scope: a typo, a missing import, or use before assignment.

l_file.title: FileNotFoundError
l_file.detail: The path doesn't exist (a subclass of OSError); check the working directory and relative paths.

title: Which SQL JOIN?
intro: Every join returns the matching rows. The choice is about which unmatched rows you also need.

q1.text: Which unmatched rows must stay in the result?

options.label: None: only rows that match in both tables
All rows from the first (left) table
All rows from the second (right) table
All rows from both tables

l_inner.title: INNER JOIN
l_inner.detail: Only matching rows. Customers without orders and orders without customers both disappear.

l_left.title: LEFT JOIN
l_left.detail: Every left row; right-side columns are NULL when nothing matches. To find customers with no orders, add `WHERE o.id IS NULL`.

l_right.title: RIGHT JOIN
l_right.detail: Every right row. The same as a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped, which most people find easier to read.

l_full.title: FULL OUTER JOIN
l_full.detail: Everything from both tables, with NULLs on whichever side has no match. Useful for reconciling two sources.

title: Which SQL clause does this filter or limit belong in?
intro: Filtering, sorting and limiting each have their own clause, decided by when in the query they apply.

options.label: Individual rows, based on column values (status = 'paid')
Groups, based on an aggregate (regions with SUM(sales) > 1000)
The order of the output
How many rows come back (top 5)
Duplicate rows in the output

l_where.title: WHERE
l_where.detail: Filters rows before grouping; it cannot contain aggregate functions.
l_where.code: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND total BETWEEN 10 AND 100;

l_having.title: HAVING
l_having.detail: Filters groups after GROUP BY, so it can use aggregates.
l_having.code:
SELECT region, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY region
HAVING SUM(total) > 1000;

l_order.title: ORDER BY
l_order.detail: Sorts the final result (ASC by default); it can use SELECT aliases.
l_order.code: SELECT region, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC;

l_limit.title: LIMIT
l_limit.detail: Caps the number of rows returned; pair it with ORDER BY for a meaningful top N. OFFSET skips rows.
l_limit.code: SELECT name, total FROM orders ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 5;

l_distinct.title: SELECT DISTINCT
l_distinct.detail: Removes duplicate rows from the output.

title: Mean, median or mode?
intro: The "typical value" depends on the data type and on outliers.

q1.text: What kind of data is it?

options.label: Categories (colour, city, plan)
Numbers

q2.text: Is the distribution skewed or does it have outliers?

options.label: Yes: incomes, house prices, delivery times
No, it's roughly symmetric

l_mode.title: Mode
l_mode.detail: The most frequent category; the only average that works for nominal data. `s.mode()` returns a Series because there can be ties.

l_median.title: Median
l_median.detail: The middle value, robust to outliers; in right-skewed data the mean lies above it.

l_mean.title: Mean
l_mean.detail: Uses every value and pairs naturally with the standard deviation; fine when data are symmetric.

title: Linear or logistic regression?
intro: It depends on what you are predicting.

options.label: A continuous number: price, revenue, temperature, time
One of two outcomes: churn / stay, fraud / genuine, pass / fail
One of three or more unordered categories

l_linear.title: Linear regression
l_linear.detail: Least squares fit of y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + …; check the LINE assumptions and R².
l_linear.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.coef_, model.intercept_, model.score(X_test, y_test))

l_logistic.title: Logistic regression
l_logistic.detail: Predicts the probability of the positive class through the log-odds; a threshold (0.5 by default) gives the class.
l_logistic.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
probs = clf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

l_multi.title: Multinomial logistic regression
l_multi.detail: Logistic regression extended to several classes; scikit-learn's LogisticRegression handles it automatically.

title: merge, concat, pivot or melt?
intro: Combining puts tables together; reshaping changes a table's layout.

options.label: Putting two or more tables together
Changing one table's layout or summarizing it
Same columns, more rows (monthly files)
Different columns that match on a key column
Different columns that match on the index
Wide → long (month columns into rows)
Long → wide, each row/column pair appears once
Long → wide, pairs repeat and need aggregating
Count how often category combinations occur

l_concat.title: pd.concat
l_concat.detail: Stacks rows (`axis=0`), aligning on column names; `ignore_index=True` renumbers.

l_merge.title: merge
l_merge.detail: Joins on key columns; inner by default. Check row counts and use `validate=` to catch duplicate keys.

l_join.title: join
l_join.detail: Joins on the index; left by default.

l_melt.title: melt
l_melt.detail: Identifier columns stay; the others become variable/value pairs.

l_pivot.title: pivot
l_pivot.detail: Pure reshape; raises an error if an index/column pair is duplicated.

l_pivot_table.title: pivot_table
l_pivot_table.detail: Reshape plus aggregation (mean by default); `fill_value` and `margins` available.
l_pivot_table.code: table = df.pivot_table(values="revenue", index="region", columns="quarter", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)

l_crosstab.title: pd.crosstab
l_crosstab.detail: A frequency table of two categorical variables; `normalize=True` for proportions.

title: [], .loc, .iloc or .at?
intro: Pick the selector by whether you know labels, positions or a condition.

q1.text: How do you identify what you want?

options.label: One or more whole columns by name
Rows by index label (and maybe columns by name)
Rows and columns by position (first row, last 3 columns)
Rows meeting a condition
A single cell, fast

l_brackets.title: Brackets: df["col"] or df[["a", "b"]]
l_brackets.detail: One name gives a Series; a list gives a DataFrame.

l_loc.title: .loc
l_loc.detail: Label-based; slices include the end label.

l_iloc.title: .iloc
l_iloc.detail: Position-based; slices exclude the end position, like Python.
l_iloc.code:
df.iloc[0]          # first row
df.iloc[:, -3:]     # last three columns

l_mask.title: Boolean mask with .loc
l_mask.detail: Filters rows, selects columns and assigns safely in one step.

l_at.title: .at / .iat
l_at.detail: Get or set a single value by label (`at`) or position (`iat`).

title: What's wrong with this model?
intro: Compare the training score with the test score, then look at how the test score was produced.

options.label: Both training and test scores are low
Training score is very high, test score much lower
Both are suspiciously high, near perfect
Both are high and close together

q2.text: Is the positive class rare (say under 10% of rows)?

options.label: Yes, and I'm judging by accuracy
No, or I already use precision and recall

l_underfit.title: Underfitting (high bias)
l_underfit.detail: The model is too simple. Add informative features, use a more flexible model, or reduce regularization.

l_overfit.title: Overfitting (high variance)
l_overfit.detail: The model memorized noise. Get more data, simplify (e.g. `max_depth`), regularize, drop weak features, and select models with cross-validation.

l_leak.title: Suspect data leakage
l_leak.detail: Check for preprocessing fitted before the split, duplicates across sets, features that encode the target, or future information.

l_imbalance.title: Accuracy is misleading
l_imbalance.detail: A model that always predicts the majority class can score high. Use precision, recall, F1 or ROC AUC, and stratify the split.

l_good.title: A good fit
l_good.detail: Similar training and test scores at a useful level. Confirm on the untouched test set once, then report it.

title: Which chart?
intro: Start from the question the chart must answer.

q1.text: What does the chart need to show?

options.label: Change over time
A comparison across categories
How one numeric variable is distributed
The relationship between two numeric variables
Correlations among many variables at once
Parts of a whole

q2.text: One group, or several groups compared?

options.label: One group: I want to see the full shape
Several groups side by side
Two to five
More than five, or several wholes to compare

l_line.title: Line chart
l_line.detail: Time on the x-axis; trends and seasonality stand out.

l_bar.title: Bar chart
l_bar.detail: Sorted bars, value axis from zero, horizontal for long labels.

l_scatter.title: Scatter plot
l_scatter.detail: Shows direction, form, strength and outliers; add a trend line with `sns.regplot`.

l_heatmap.title: Correlation heatmap
l_heatmap.detail: A diverging palette centred on 0 with annotated values.
l_heatmap.code: sns.heatmap(df.corr(numeric_only=True), annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1)

l_hist.title: Histogram
l_hist.detail: Shows shape, skew and modality; try more than one bin width.

l_box.title: Side-by-side box plots
l_box.detail: Compare medians, spreads and outliers across groups at a glance.

l_pie.title: Pie chart (sparingly)
l_pie.detail: Acceptable for two to five parts of one whole; label the percentages.

l_stacked.title: Stacked or 100% stacked bar
l_stacked.detail: Compares composition across several wholes; far easier to read than many pies.

title: Which colour palette?
intro: The palette type follows from the data, and every choice should survive colour blindness.

options.label: Separate, unordered groups (regions, products)
Ordered values from low to high (population, sales)
Values above and below a meaningful midpoint (correlation, change vs target)
One series to highlight among many

l_qual.title: Qualitative palette
l_qual.detail: Distinct hues of similar strength, few of them; colour-blind-safe options include Seaborn's "colorblind".

l_seq.title: Sequential palette
l_seq.detail: Light to dark in one hue family; viridis is perceptually uniform and colour-blind-safe.

l_div.title: Diverging palette
l_div.detail: Two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint; set `center=0` (or `vmin`/`vmax`) so the midpoint means something.

l_highlight.title: Accent plus grey
l_highlight.detail: Draw the series that matters in a strong colour and the rest in grey, and name it in the title.
